Utterly
ut'ter-lē
adv. (wholly, entirely; rendering the Hebrew infinitive absolute and charam, Greek holos)
From utter, outermost or complete, from Saxon utera, outer. In the Authorized Version it very often renders the Hebrew infinitive absolute — a verb doubled for emphasis — and elsewhere the verb charam, to devote a thing irrevocably to destruction.

Biblical Definition

Utterly means wholly, without remainder, and it is the translators' usual device for the Hebrew habit of doubling a verb for emphasis. It is used of a father's absolute refusal in the law of seduction: “If her father utterly refuse to give her unto him, he shall pay money according to the dowry of virgins” (Exodus 22:17) — the daughter protected by a right of veto that money cannot override. It is used of God's promise to destroy idols without exception, in a sentence of four words: “And the idols he shall utterly abolish” (Isaiah 2:18). It is used of judgment on nations that will not serve (Isaiah 60:12). And in one of the great sentences of the Old Testament it is used in the negative, of what God refused to do to a people who had earned it: “Nevertheless for thy great mercies' sake thou didst not utterly consume them, nor forsake them; for thou art a gracious and merciful God” (Nehemiah 9:31).

Webster 1828 Definition

Wholly; entirely; without remainder. In Scripture it commonly renders the Hebrew doubling of a verb for emphasis, and its most important use is a negative one: God did not utterly consume a people who deserved it.

expand to see more

UTTERLY, adv. [from utter, Sax. utera, outer.] Fully; completely; entirely; wholly.

2. Without exception or remainder; as, utterly destroyed.

3. It renders the Hebrew infinitive absolute, in which a verb is doubled for emphasis.

4. UTTER, a. Complete; total; final; as, utter ruin.

5. In Scripture, the idols he shall utterly abolish, Isa. 2; thou didst not utterly consume them, Neh. 9.

Key Scripture

Exodus 22:17 — "If her father utterly refuse to give her unto him, he shall pay money according to the dowry of virgins."

Isaiah 2:18 — "And the idols he shall utterly abolish."

Nehemiah 9:31 — "Nevertheless for thy great mercies' sake thou didst not utterly consume them, nor forsake them; for thou art a gracious and merciful God."

Isaiah 60:12 — "For the nation and kingdom that will not serve thee shall perish; yea, those nations shall be utterly wasted."

Modern Corruption

The absolute language of judgment is read as evidence of a cruel God, while the equally absolute language of mercy in the same books goes unread. Nehemiah 9 holds both, and holds them in the right order.

expand to see more

Nehemiah 9 is a national confession, and it is unsparing about the nation. It rehearses centuries of rebellion — they were disobedient, they cast the law behind their backs, they slew the prophets — and it does not soften a single item. Then comes the clause: Nevertheless for thy great mercies' sake thou didst not utterly consume them, nor forsake them; for thou art a gracious and merciful God. The mercy is not asserted instead of the guilt but on top of it, and it is grounded in God's character rather than in any extenuating circumstance. That is the shape of every honest confession.

The absolute language of destruction has its own context and it is judicial. Charam, the verb behind much of it, means to devote irrevocably — a thing placed beyond recovery or use, whether for destruction or for the sanctuary. The Canaanite cities were so devoted after four centuries of divine forbearance, for practices Leviticus 18 catalogues, and Israel was warned she would be treated the same and afterward was. What Scripture never does is present God as capricious. The forbearance is always longer than anyone would grant, and the judgment always later than anyone would defer it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew emphasises by the infinitive absolute, doubling the verb (dying thou shalt die); charam means to devote irrevocably, giving the noun cherem, a devoted thing. Greek uses holos and pantelos for completeness.

expand to see more

Hebrew infinitive absolute — a verb repeated in the absolute form for emphasis, usually rendered by surely or utterly.

Hebrew charam (H2763) — to devote irrevocably, to ban; used of cities and spoil placed beyond recovery.

Hebrew cherem (H2764) — a devoted thing, a ban; the noun behind the Achan narrative in Joshua 7.

Hebrew kalah (H3615) — to complete, to consume entirely; the verb God did not carry out in Nehemiah 9:31.

Greek pantelos (G3838) — completely, to the uttermost; able also to save them to the uttermost.

Usage

"Of an absolute paternal refusal protecting a daughter: If her father utterly refuse to give her unto him (Exodus 22:17)."

"Of idols abolished without exception: And the idols he shall utterly abolish (Isaiah 2:18)."

"Of mercy withholding a deserved end: thou didst not utterly consume them, nor forsake them (Nehemiah 9:31)."
